Protective Apparel, Barriers, and Shields, and How They Are Tested

Unit 2: Radiation, Magnetic, and Facility Safety. Lesson 8 of 60 in CRES Academy.

Apparel and barriers are the only safety equipment in the department that a technician both tests and condemns, and they fail silently: a torn apron looks exactly like a good one.

Lead equivalent

Protective garments are rated by the thickness of lead that would attenuate as well as the material in them.

Aprons and gloves      0.25, 0.5, and 1 mm lead equivalent; 0.25 mm the minimum, 0.5 mm the normal choice
At 75 kVp              0.25 mm attenuates about 66 percent, 1 mm about 99 percent
Weight                 a 1 mm apron can weigh 12 kg (25 lb), which is why 0.5 mm is the usual compromise
Thyroid, gonadal, eyewear  read the lead equivalent marked on the garment and record it
Bucky slot cover and fluoroscopic curtain  each at least 0.25 mm; the cover closes a gap of about 5 cm at gonadal level

Storage and inspection

Hang garments on racks, never fold them, because a fold cracks the lead and the crack is invisible from outside. Inspect and image every apron, glove, thyroid shield, and gonadal shield at least annually, by fluoroscopy or by radiography at about 120 kVp and 10 mAs, and look for cracks, bunching along fold lines, tears, and holes. Replace on any defect in a critical area, record the garment's identifier and the result, and physically remove a failed garment from the room, because an apron that fails inspection and stays on the rack will be worn.

Barriers

  • A primary barrier intercepts the useful beam. The fluoroscopic receptor assembly is one, at least 2 mm lead equivalent, interlocked so the tube cannot energize while it is parked out of position.
  • A secondary barrier intercepts scatter and leakage: the control booth, the lead glass window, and the upper walls. A booth barrier is about 1/16 inch lead equivalent, and the booth partition has to be placed and sized so that nothing but scattered radiation can reach the operator behind it.
  • Mobile shields fill the gap in rooms where staff must stand at the table, and a mobile exposure switch must reach 2 m from the tube.

Room design, at recognition level

A medical physicist designs shielding from four inputs: the workload of the room, the use factor (how much of the time the beam points that way), the occupancy factor (who is on the other side of that wall and for how long), and the distance. The output is a shielding report that says what goes in each wall, floor, ceiling, and door. Keep it with the room record, because any penetration you make through a wall for a cable is a change to that design and has to be sealed the way the report says.

Gonadal shields and collimation

Gonadal shields come as shadow shields hung in the beam, flat contact shields laid on the patient, and shaped shields for male anatomy. Used properly they cut ovary dose about 50 percent and testicular dose about 95 percent, and they are used whenever they will not cover the region of interest, within about 0.5 cm of the primary beam. But the first shield is always collimation: tissue outside the field gets only scatter, so a working collimator lamp and an accurate light field do more for dose than any garment.

Exam tip: 0.25 mm lead equivalent is the minimum and 0.5 mm the normal apron; inspect apparel at least annually by imaging it and retire it on any crack or tear; hang, never fold. Primary barriers take the useful beam, secondary barriers take scatter and leakage, and collimation is the first shield.
Remember
Aprons and gloves run 0.25, 0.5, and 1 mm lead equivalent with 0.25 the minimum and 0.5 the normal pick, thyroid and gonadal shields carry a marked value, bucky slot covers and curtains at least 0.25 mm; hang them, image them at least annually at about 120 kVp and 10 mAs, and retire on any crack; primary barriers take the useful beam at 2 mm and the booth is about 1/16 inch; and workload, use factor, and occupancy factor drive the physicist's shielding design while collimation stays the first shield.
Deeper explanation

Protective Apparel, Barriers, and Shields, and How They Are Tested, explained slowly

Apparel is the safety equipment you both test and condemn

Nothing else in the department fails as invisibly as a lead apron. A cracked one looks, feels, and weighs the same as a good one, and the person wearing it has no way to know. That is why the inspection is an imaging test and why a failed garment must physically leave the room.

Aprons and gloves           0.25, 0.5, and 1 mm        0.25 mm is the minimum; 0.5 mm is the
                                                       normal choice
At 75 kVp                   0.25 mm attenuates about   a 1 mm apron can weigh 12 kg (25 lb), which
                            66 percent, 1 mm about     is why 0.5 mm is the working compromise
                            99 percent
Thyroid, gonadal shields,   marked on the garment      read it, record it, and inspect it like
leaded eyewear                                         an apron

Attenuation is never total: an apron is two half-value layers at most, which is why distance still matters while wearing one and why nobody stands in the primary beam in an apron.

The inspection, step by step

  1. Inventory every garment with a unique identifier, its lead equivalent, and its location, in the CMMS or the physicist's log.
  2. Inspect by hand first: feel along fold lines and seams, check the closures and the stitching, look at the neck and shoulder where the weight hangs.
  3. Image each garment at least annually, by fluoroscopy or by radiography at about 120 kVp and 10 mAs, laid flat.
  4. Look for cracks and bunching along fold lines, tears, holes, and thinning at the shoulders. A fluoroscopic sweep finds the big defects fast; a radiograph documents them.
  5. Judge by location and size: a small defect at the hem is not a critical-area defect, while any hole over the thyroid, gonads, or a shield's working area retires the garment.
  6. Record the identifier, the date, the method, and pass or fail, then physically remove failures from the department. A garment that failed and stayed on the rack will be worn by somebody.
  7. Store hanging on racks. Folding cracks lead, and the crack does not show from outside.

Barriers, primary and secondary

A primary barrier is anything that intercepts the useful beam: the wall a tube points at, the fluoroscopic receptor assembly, the chest stand's backing. A secondary barrier intercepts only scatter and leakage: the booth, the lead glass, upper walls. Secondary barriers can be much thinner, which is why the booth figure is a fraction of the receptor assembly's. Mobile shields on stands fill the gaps in rooms where staff must be at the table, and they work only if they are between the person and the patient, which is where scatter comes from.

Room design, at recognition level

The physicist's shielding report is computed from four inputs:

Workload          how much the room is used, in milliampere-minutes per week
Use factor        what fraction of the beam-on time the tube points at that barrier
Occupancy factor  how much of the time someone is on the far side, and who they are
Distance          from the source to the occupied point, squared, as always

The output tells the builder what goes in each wall, floor, ceiling, door, and window. Keep that report with the room record, because a cable penetration you make through a shielded wall is a change to the design and has to be sealed the way the report specifies, with a documented survey afterward.

Gonadal shielding and the first shield

Shadow shields hang in the beam and cast a shadow on the patient; flat contact shields lie on the patient; shaped shields enclose male anatomy. Used properly they cut ovary dose about 50 percent and testicular dose about 95 percent, and they are indicated whenever they will not cover the region of interest, within about 0.5 cm of the primary beam. But the first and best shield is collimation: tissue outside the field only ever receives scatter, so an accurate light field is worth more than any garment. That makes the collimator lamp a dose-critical part, and a burned-out lamp an urgent call rather than a cosmetic one.

What to memorize

  • 0.25 mm minimum, 0.5 mm normal for aprons and gloves; bucky slot cover and curtain at least 0.25 mm; receptor assembly at least 2 mm; booth about 1/16 inch.
  • Inspect at least annually by imaging, about 120 kVp and 10 mAs; retire on cracks, tears, or holes in critical areas; hang, never fold.
  • Primary barriers take the useful beam, secondary barriers take scatter and leakage.
  • Workload, use factor, occupancy factor, and distance drive shielding design.
  • Gonadal shielding cuts ovary dose about 50 percent and testicular about 95 percent; collimation is the first shield.
